Suicide rates among middle-aged Americans have risen sharply in the past decade, prompting concern that a generation of baby boomers who have faced years of economic worry and easy access to prescription painkillers may be particularly vulnerable to self-inflicted harm.
More people now die of suicide than in car accidents, according to theCenters for Disease Control and Prevention, which published the findings in Friday’sissueof its Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. In 2010 there were 33,687 deaths from motor vehicle crashes and 38,364 suicides.
Suicide has typically been viewed as a problem of teenagers and the elderly, and the surge in suicide rates among middle-aged Americans is surprising.
From 1999 to 2010, the suicide rate among Americans ages 35 to 64 rose by nearly 30 percent, to 17.6 deaths per 100,000 people, up from 13.7. Although suicide rates are growing among both middle-aged men and women, far more men take their own lives. The suicide rate for middle-aged men was 27.3 deaths per 100,000, while for women it was 8.1 deaths per 100,000.
The most pronounced increases were seen among men in their 50s, a group in which suicide rates jumped by nearly 50 percent, to about 30 per 100,000. For women, the largest increase was seen in those ages 60 to 64, among whom rates increased by nearly 60 percent, to 7.0 per 100,000.
Suicide rates can be difficult to interpret because of variations in the way local officials report causes of death. But C.D.C. and academic researchers said they were confident that the data documented an actual increase in deaths by suicide and not a statistical anomaly. While reporting of suicides is not always consistent around the country, the current numbers are, if anything, too low.
“It’s vastly underreported,” said Julie Phillips, an associate professor of sociology at Rutgers University who has published research on rising suicide rates. “We know we’re not counting all suicides.”
The reasons for suicide are often complex, and officials and researchers acknowledge that no one can explain with certainty what is behind the rise. But C.D.C. officials cited a number of possible explanations, including that as adolescents people in this generation also posted higher rates of suicide compared with other cohorts.
“It is the baby boomer group where we see the highest rates of suicide,” said the C.D.C.’s deputy director, Ileana Arias. “There may be something about that group, and how they think about life issues and their life choices that may make a difference.”
The rise in suicides may also stem from the economic downturn over the past decade. Historically, suicide rates rise during times of financial stress and economic setbacks. “The increase does coincide with a decrease in financial standing for a lot of families over the same time period,” Dr. Arias said.
Another factor may be the widespread availability of opioid drugs like OxyContin and oxycodone, which can be particularly deadly in large doses.
Although most suicides are still committed using firearms, officials said there was a marked increase in poisoning deaths, which include intentional overdoses of prescription drugs, and hangings. Poisoning deaths were up 24 percent over all during the 10-year period and hangings were up 81 percent.
Dr. Arias noted that the higher suicide rates might be due to a series of life and financial circumstances that are unique to the baby boomer generation. Men and women in that age group are often coping with the stress of caring for aging parents while still providing financial and emotional support to adult children.
“Their lives are configured a little differently than it has been in the past for that age group,” Dr. Arias said. “It may not be that they are more sensitive or that they have a predisposition to suicide, but that they may be dealing with more.”
Preliminary research at Rutgers suggests that the risk for suicide is unlikely to abate for future generations. Changes in marriage, social isolation and family roles mean many of the pressures faced by baby boomers will continue in the next generation, Dr. Phillips said.
“The boomers had great expectations for what their life might look like, but I think perhaps it hasn’t panned out that way,” she said. “All these conditions the boomers are facing, future cohorts are going to be facing many of these conditions as well.”
Nancy Berliner, a Boston historian, lost her 58-year-old husband to suicide nearly two years ago. She said that while the reasons for his suicide were complex, she would like to see more attention paid to prevention and support for family members who lose someone to suicide.

It has been an unusually soft free-agent market this year. There could be multiple reasons for that: the salary cap’s lack of growth, a deep pool of draft prospects at the same positions that are deep in free agency (defensive end, for example), a subtle leaguewide shift in the way free agents are viewed, perhaps. Whatever the case, it’s left a lot of really good buys on the market. True, every unsigned veteran has a flaw or two. (After all, there’s a reason he’s still unsigned.) But a lot of these players still have valuable attributes that can fill an important niche for a team. These unsigned veterans should not be viewed in terms of what they once were; they should be viewed in terms of what they are now. Here are 10 who are worth signing:
Pass rushers
No position this year has drawn more disappointing prices in free agency than defensive line. The headliner Cliff Avril kicked things off with a shockingly small $4.5 million bonus in Seattle, and the rest of the market followed suit in futility. One would guess that’d change after Elvis Dumervil’s surprising five-year, $26 million deal from the supposedly cash-poor Ravens. But more than 48 hours later, three familiar names remained unsigned:
DE Dwight Freeney
His measly 2012 sack total of five suggests he’s slowing down. The film disagrees. Freeney still transitions from speed to power as effectively as just about any edge player in the game. True, it now takes him a split second longer to build up that speed. But being a 12-year veteran who has always played with great leverage, Freeney knows how to compensate for his mild declines. The sacks may not be there but the ability to collapse the pocket still is.
DE John Abraham
Years or various injuries make Abraham a more limited player than Freeney. Whoever signs him might not even bother trying to play him on first and second down. On third down, though, Abraham can still turn the corner. Plus, he’s always redirected well in space, which suggests he could be a serviceable weak-outside linebacker in a 3-4 (perhaps even on some first and second downs).
OLB Shaun Phillips
He’s lanky, fluid and still only 32. Perhaps he isn’t a true No. 1 edge rusher, but as he showed early in his career playing opposite Shawne Merriman, he can be a destructive No. 2. That includes against the run, mainly as a backside chaser. There was little sign of Phillips’s speed declining last year, yet for some reason the current market is treating him like the soon-to-be 35-year-old James Harrison (a star who
is
slowing down).
Run defenders
DT Richard Seymour
Injuries took a bit of a toll on Seymour last year, but the former Raider still has the strength and technical savvy to win in a phone booth, especially as a 5-technique (which a lot of 3-4 defenses currently have needs for).
DT Alan Branch
He may have been forever stigmatized as an underachiever after his lackluster time in Arizona. But the last two years in Seattle, Branch was a vital part of an upper-tier run defense. The difference there was he often played the 3-technique, meaning he was shooting gaps instead of combating double teams. The 325-plus-pounder didn’t begin to post quality 3-technique numbers, but in that role he wound up having the same type of run-stuffing impact that a quality nose tackle would have had. In other words, Branch must be evaluated on film, not paper. At 28, he is in his prime and capable of buttressing an interior 4-3 rotation.
ILB Karlos Dansby
At 31, he still has athleticism. And he’ll always be a smart player. Not only is he productive against the run, but he’s also one of the better short-area pass defending linebackers in the game. Danby could, at the very least, enhance a team’s nickel and dime packages. Those sub-packages are where today’s great defenses thrive.
Pass defenders
DB Charles Woodson
This is the most baffling one of all. How can no team want Woodson as a plug-and-play Band-Aid right now? Yes, he’s 36 and missed most of last season with a shoulder injury. But at 35 he was a firm Pro Bowler thanks to his dominance as a utility rover in the box.
That’s
where fans fail to recognize Woodson’s value. In him they see a cornerback who can no longer play man-to-man. But what he really is is a safety who can drop into deep centerfield or, more pertinently, knife through the box. He understands angles and offensive designs as well as anyone in the league. If a defense were to add Woodson, it’d instantly become more multiple and disguisable. That makes everyone on D better. This alone makes Woodson worth signing.
DB DeAngelo Hall
He’s a more stale version of Woodson, but he has less mileage. One reason the 2012 Redskin defense survived with no pass rush and a depleted secondary was they were able to use Hall at every different secondary position imaginable. Hall can be arrogant, but as with Woodson or Ronde Barber, his versatility and awareness as a mid-30s-year-old nickelback can patch a lot of holes over the course of a season.
Offensive Linemen
RT Eric Winston
He may be the best right tackle in the N.F.L. He moves well in zone run blocking; he doesn’t always need help in pass protection (unlike a lot of right tackles); and he’s a respected voice in the locker room.
RT Andre Smith
In contrast, Smith is a less-respected voice in the locker room but a much more gifted player than Winston. He has rare initial burst for a man who is built like a small house. The problem is, he doesn’t show it on a consistent basis. But most of the league’s right tackles can’t show what Smith shows on
any
basis. To Smith’s credit, the past two years, when he has hit his inevitable lulls, he at least hasn’t been an outright liability.

Obama Bets on Rice's Redemption:The Times's Mark Landler discusses the White House's decision to put Susan E. Rice back in the harsh spotlight as the national security adviser.
WASHINGTON â President Obama announced on Wednesday afternoon that Susan E. Rice, the American ambassador to the United Nations, would replace Tom Donilon, who is resigning, as national security adviser in a major shakeup of his foreign-policy inner circle.
President Obama on Wednesday announced that Susan E. Rice, right, would replace Tom Donilon, second from right, as national security adviser. Samantha Powers, left, will take Ms. Rice's position as the American ambassador to the United Nations.
The appointment, which Mr. Obama made in a Rose Garden ceremony, puts Ms. Rice, 48, an outspoken diplomat and a close political ally, at the heart of the administrationâs foreign-policy apparatus.
It is also a defiant gesture to Republicans who harshly criticized Ms. Rice for presenting an erroneous account of the deadly attacks on the American mission in Benghazi, Libya. The post of national security adviser, while powerful, does not require Senate confirmation.
In his announcement, Mr. Obama referred to Ms. Riceâs role as an adviser during his 2008 presidential campaign and praised her work as a key diplomat during his first term.
âWith her background as a scholar, Susan understands that thereâs no substitute for American leadership,â Mr. Obama said. âShe is at once passionate and pragmatic. I think everybody understands Susan is a fierce champion for justice and human dignity, but sheâs also mindful that we have to exercise our power wisely and deliberately.â
Mr. Obama also named Samantha Power, a National Security Council official, as Ms. Riceâs replacement at the United Nations. Ms. Power, who has written extensively about genocide, is closely allied with Ms. Rice on human rights issues.
In his statement, Mr. Obama cited Ms. Powerâs work with Ms. Rice on issues related to the United Nations.
âShe knows the U.N.'s strengths. She knows its weaknesses," Mr. Obama said. "She knows that American interests are advanced when we can rally the world to our side. And she knows that we have to stand up for the things that we believe in. And to ensure that we have the principled leadership we need at the United Nations, I would strongly urge the Senate to confirm her without delay.â
Mr. Donilon, 58, a central member of Mr. Obamaâs foreign-policy team since he first took office, has exerted sweeping influence, mostly behind the scenes, on issues from counterterrorism to the reorientation of America to Asia from the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
âTomâs that rare combination of the strategic and the tactical. He has a strategic sense of where we need to go, and he has a tactical sense of how to get there,â Mr. Obama said in his announcement. âHeâs helped shape every single national security policy of my presidency, from forging a new national security strategy rooted in our economic strength here at home to ending the war in Iraq.â
Among Mr. Donilonâs last big projects was negotiating the highly unusual informal meeting between Mr. Obama and President Xi Jinping of China on Friday at an estate in Southern California. Just back from talks in Beijing, he clearly took pride of ownership.
âI donât know when there was a broad meeting like this,â Mr. Donilon said in an interview. âFor the last 40 years or so, these conversations have taken place in a more formal, scripted context.â
But Mr. Donilon has also hit a rough patch recently, with the publication ofan unflattering profilein Foreign Policy magazine that cast him as a sharp-elbowed infighter and a domineering boss who had strained relationships with colleagues, including his former deputy, Denis R. McDonough, now the White House chief of staff.
Mr. Donilon and Mr. McDonough, however, both denied those reports. Mr. McDonough said he had a âvery good relationship with Tom,â adding, âIt pains me to think anybody would think heâs leaving because of me.â
Mr. Donilon, whose departure is effective in early July, said he had planned to leave after Mr. Obamaâs first term but stayed on at the presidentâs request to break in a new team led by Secretary of State John Kerry, Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel, and the director of the Central Intelligence Agency, John O. Brennan.

WASHINGTON â After years ofcriticismof the wireless service on its trains, Amtrak announced on Thursday that it had upgraded its cellular-based Wi-Fi using broadband technologies that will improve the speed and reliability of the Internet in its passenger cars.
Follow@NYTNationalfor breaking news and headlines.
Amtrakâs Wi-Fi has been the target of technology jokes since the railroad introduced the service, with some passengers comparing it to dial-up services like America Online or Prodigy. But others have praised the service, saying it allows them to be productive while traveling between cities, unlike airline travel. Because of the technical difficulties of maintaining a strong Internet connection on a moving train, the increase in speed would still be less than most people experience at home.
The railroad said thebroadband upgradewas complete on the high-speed Acela trains that travel the more than 400 miles between Washington and Boston. Several state-supported routes in California, including the Capitol Corridor, Pacific Surfliner and San Joaquin routes, have also been upgraded.
Amtrak said it would roll out the upgrades to all remaining Amtrak trains equipped with Wi-Fi, including the Northeast Regional, by late summer.
âWe continue to place a strong focus on improving customer satisfaction, and this upgrade is delivering the improved speeds and connectivity required to maintain a competitive edge,â Deborah Stone-Wulf, Amtrakâs chief of sales distribution and customer service, said in a statement.
Amtrak said Acela passengers have already noticed an improvement in the Wi-Fi service aboard the trains and have been commenting through social media.
But not all the social media chatter has been positive.
Shelton Mercer, chief executive ofTwitChange, an Atlanta-based Web site that brings celebrities and fans together for good causes,wrote on Twitterlast month, â#Amtrak âWi-fiâ should be renamed âWhy-Try.âÂ â
Amtrak responded to some negative Twitter posts, saying the upgrades would strengthen its Wi-Fi network and increase the amount of bandwidth available for tech-savvy passengers who have become accustomed to being connected while traveling.
Sara Wachter-Boettcher, an author and Web consultant in Lancaster, Pa., called the service an infuriating luxury. On a recent trip home from teaching a workshop in New York, she said, she was desperately trying to catch up on e-mail. But the Wi-Fi on the train booted her off every few minutes, she said, and she had to resort to a combination of her smartphone and laptop to keep working.
âOn the one hand, weâre lucky to have such pervasive Internet access,â she said in an e-mail. âOn the other, itâs frustrating anytime something that should work doesnât.â
Unlike most airlines, Amtrak said it would continue to provide free Wi-Fi service. The railroad said that Wi-Fi was available on trains that serve 75 percent of Amtrak passengers, and that it routinely supported 30 percent to 50 percent of passengers on a given train.
But Amtrak also said it would continue to limit some Internet activities.
To ensure that all passengers have an opportunity to use the Wi-Fi service, Amtrak said, it would still restrict data-heavy activities that could slow the service down, like streaming video sites like Netflix and music sites like Pandora. The railroad also restricts file downloads larger than 10MB.
Even with the upgrades, Amtrak will continue to face some challenges with its wireless service. High-speed service is not available everywhere, and because the railroad uses different carriers along its routes, including Verizon and AT&T, service could still be interrupted or slowed as the Wi-Fi signals switch between the carriers. In addition, as the speed of the service increases, so will the number of people trying to use it, potentially slowing it down.
Still, Amtrak seems confident that passengers will have a better Internet experience aboard its trains. In a news release announcing the upgrades, the railroad suggested the following Twitter post: âProductivity on @Amtrak #Acela just got better. Their onboard #Wi-Fi is now powered by 4G technology.â

It has been more than three weeks since Avonte Oquendo, an autistic 14-year-old, slipped out the front door of his high school in Long Island City, Queens, and disappeared without a trace.

There are signs with pictures of him posted on tollbooths at the mouth of the Queens-Midtown Tunnel and in languages from Russian to Bengali all over New York City. There have been loudspeaker announcements throughout the subway system, scent-sniffing bloodhounds, volunteer foot patrols and daily scans of rooftops by police helicopters. Several of them have buzzed over Queens most days since Avonte went missing. And every day, dozens of police officers fan out across a wide region, checking buildings, lots and even trash bins.
The Police Department has received more than 450 leads related to Avonteâs disappearance, and detectives have investigated and ruled out all but 48, Police Commissioner Raymond W. Kelly said at a news conference on Friday. He added that detectives were still in the process of viewing 196 pieces of video.
Avonte, he said, had not appeared on any of the video clips that investigators had watched so far.
On Thursday, in remarks to a television station, Mr. Kelly expressed fears that Avonte was dead. âUnfortunately, we are not hopeful that weâre going to find this young man alive, but we are continuing our search,â he told WABC-TV.
The comment infuriated members of Avonteâs family, who on Friday said they were afraid that the comments might make the public less vigilant.
âThere is no evidence that Avonte is not alive,â said David H. Perecman, a lawyer for the family.
The family is suing the city on grounds that the Riverview School, which opened this year at 1-50 51st Avenue in Long Island City, did not have safety features like alarmed doors or proper monitoring systems, and suffered a breakdown in the protocol for dealing with Avonte, who was known to run off periodically.
At a news conference beside the familyâs makeshift search command center, at the foot of 51st Avenue where it dead ends at the East River, Mr. Perecman said the commissionerâs words were âreckless.â
Asked in an interview on Friday whether he thought Avonte was still alive, Mr. Kelly said, âWe certainly hope so.â
Nowhere is Avonteâs absence felt more acutely than in a tent at the command center , near the school he stepped out of on Oct. 4, where Avonteâs mother, Vanessa Fontaine, has spent her days. She was there to shepherd volunteers who have come in droves â and because it is too painful to be home, in the silent shadow of her childâs absence.
âItâs very quiet,â she said. âNothing to say, no, âAvonte, what are you doing?â Itâs not the same. Iâd rather be here than be at home.â
For weeks police boats have plied the waters and divers have searched the East River, while volunteers from organizations as varied as churches and motorcycle clubs have combed the streets. There are 80 detectives working the case. At times a recording of his motherâs voice was blasted from roving search vehicles calling out to Avonte, who because of his condition is nonverbal. He cannot care for himself or even tie his own shoes.
âAt this juncture we have nothing that we could say is a confirmed sighting of the young man,â Mr. Kelly said on Friday.
As autumn weather has descended on the city, the volunteers have begun to fade away, and the police have indicated that the search efforts will be scaled back.
Ms. Fontaine and Avonteâs father, Daniel Oquendo, have not given up hope. âHe is not gone,â Ms. Fontaine said. âI donât know what the commissioner was thinking of. Heâs alive, heâs out there.â
After the conference, Ms. Fontaine returned to her vigil. âItâs like a nightmare,â she said. âYou ever had that dream and said, âIâm so happy I woke up from this and it was a dream?â I wish this was a dream and I could go home and see Avonte in that room in that house.

Ideally, Congress would raise the federal minimum wage above the paltry $7.25 an hour. But since there is little chance of that happening soon, it is up to the states to provide relief for low-wage workers. Nineteen states and the District of Columbia have so far increased the minimum wage above the federal level. Tuesday will be New Jerseyâs chance to do the same.
For Op-Ed, follow@nytopinionand to hear from the editorial page
editor, Andrew Rosenthal, follow@andyrNYT.
Voters in New Jersey should adopt a constitutional amendment (Public Question 2) that raises the minimum wage to $8.25 an hour starting on Jan. 1. If it is approved, more than 400,000 people now working at or near minimum wage could benefit. The amendment would also adjust the wage yearly based on inflation, as several other states do.
Gov. Chris Christie and the business community have opposed this amendment. Business leaders say, as they often do, that such increases would cost jobs. But a recent study by New Jersey Policy Perspectiveestimatedthat because the working poor spend virtually every extra dollar they earn, the increase in pay would add $175 million to the economy in 2014, most of it in New Jersey. Mr. Christie has said he supports a $1-an-hour increase phased in over three years, and vetoed a bill that raised the wage in one step. His approach is far too slow a pace to help people at the bottom of the economic ladder.
Other states have already moved to increase the wages for workers with the lowest incomes. New York has approved a law raising the minimum in steps until wages reach $9 an hour by the end of 2015. Washington State already has a $9.19 minimum. Vermontâs minimum is $8.60. California will go to $10 an hour by 2016. New Jersey residents should follow suit and help struggling families by voting Tuesday to raise the stateâs minimum wage.

PARIS — When Bernard Tomic took the court for his first-round match Tuesday, he was in a rare position for a professional athlete: much more attention was focused on who was in the crowd than who was on the clay.
Down two sets to Victor Hanescu, Bernard Tomic retired from his match Tuesday because of a hamstring injury.
Tomic’s father and coach, John,was barredlast week from attending the French Open, even if he bought a ticket and tried to enter with the other fans. Hewas arrestedin Madrid earlier this month, accused of assaulting his son’s training partner, Thomas Drouet.
The question Tuesday was whether John Tomic would try to sneak in to see Bernard, a rising Australian star, and what tournament officials would do if he was spotted in the modest stands that surround Court 6. The mystery made a meeting between the 61st-ranked Tomic, 20, and the 54th-ranked Victor Hanescu a must-see match for the TMZ age, even in a sport whose history has been dotted with abusive parents.
Tomic said that his father was in Paris, but apparently he stayed back at the hotel. Moments after the match started, though, Bernard had another, more prosaic, drama to deal with.
On the second point of the match, he felt a tearing in his right hamstring. He grabbed the back of his leg and grimaced as he continued to play, and he received treatment on the court after three games. He lost the first two sets, 5-7, 6-7 (8), the second in a tiebreaker after a rain delay of 70 minutes. Tomic then retired after the first three games of the third set, trailing, 1-2.
So much about Tomic is head-scratching, and this moment was no different. When he approached Hanescu to shake his hand, Tomic chatted with him and smiled. Then, before leaving the court, he signed a few autographs.
By the time Tomic met with reporters, he had turned serious again. He opened his news conference with a statement, his first extensive public remarks on his father since the Madrid incident.
“He’s here right now in Paris so, you know, he’s still working with me, he’s still my dad, he’s still my coach and, you know, I love him a lot,” said Tomic, who had not played a match since losing in the first round in Madrid.
Tomic did not want to talk about the incident in Madrid, saying only that it was difficult for him.
Later in the news conference, after he said a doctor told him the hamstring tear would keep him out a week or two, Tomic said he was considering hiring an outside person to help with his training, “not sort of a coach but someone just to help me a little bit.”
Tomic said he had not decided whom that person would be, but that perhaps it would come before the grass-court season begins in the run-up to Wimbledon. Tomic said his father would always be his coach because he knows his game better than anyone. But when asked if he was concerned that someone would be reluctant to take the job, given his father’s reputation, Tomic smiled.
“No, I’ve thought about it,” he said. “I probably, you know, have a choice of two or three people now. I will decide that with my dad over the next week, and you know, who knows? Maybe you’ll see someone you don’t expect.”
Whomever it is, Tomic will need him. For several years, he has been considered one of tennis’s most promising players. But in the wake of the Madrid accusations, the ATP Tour and the International Tennis Federation announced that they would not give credentials to his father for any of their tournaments. On Tuesday, Johnny Perkins, a spokesman for the All-England Club, said in an e-mail that Wimbledon would not give John Tomic a credential and would bar him from the grounds.
That leaves Tomic essentially alone at his matches. Drouet, who said after the Madrid incident that he had also seen John strike Bernard, is also in Paris, but according to the French newspaper L’Équipe, he is working with Marion Bartoli of France.
Tomic said that he was able to let such things go and that he thought he had been training well before the French Open. He added that his father’s absence was not a problem during the match Tuesday as much as not being able to feel his right leg.
But Tomic also acknowledged his bumpy career trajectory, saying he had not yet fulfilled his potential.
“I’ve experienced where I didn’t have to defend nothing and when I got up there it was very easy and comfortable, I was very relaxed,” he said. “But then it became difficult to sort of defend stuff. I got nervous, a little bit of pressure, and I didn’t quite handle it well. Came the time again where I turned it around and I played well and, you know, I showed that I can play, but this is the problem at a young age, you’re up and down.”
He was down again Tuesday, albeit with an awkward smile and few moments of disarming candor. On Wednesday, Tomic said, he and his father will leave Paris for Monaco, where Bernard trains, to prepare for the grasscourt season.

Deborah A. Roma
Lopez’s alarm goes off at 3:45 a.m. every day. There is a rhythm and routine to working with horses daily.
LOUISVILLE, Ky. — They are often the unknowns. Even when they stand right in front of thousands, few know grooms’ names or acknowledge them. Yet they know more about the horse at the end of their lead line than anyone else at the racetrack.  Often, by the time the horse is loaded into the starting gate, their groom has already spent more than nine hours by their side that day.
Dagoberto Lopez, 55, is a groom and proud member of the Doug O’Neill barn. He is in charge of several horses, including Goldencents and Handsome Mike. Goldencents, who ran recently in the Kentucky Derby, is the winner of the Santa Anita Derby and the Sham Stakes. Handsome Mike won the 2012 Pennsylvania Derby.
Lopez is a personable man with expressive eyes and a gentle manner.  He willingly answered my questions in Spanish, with the help of Leandro Mora (O’Neill’s assistant trainer) as an interpreter.
Lopez’s alarm goes off at 3:45 a.m. There is a rhythm and routine to working with horses daily. He arrives and takes the bandages off the horses’ legs looking for heat, swelling or soreness. Making sure that they ate everything, he checks their temperatures. Attitude, physicality, dietary and intestinal aspects are all noted and reported.  Horses walk the shed row before going to the track under careful surveillance. After a morning workout, jog or breeze, it’s bath time.  Lopez says that Goldencents loves being bathed  and demonstrates it by a long stretch of his neck. I asked if Goldencents speaks Spanish, and he grinned and said, “Yes, Goldencents is bilingual.”
It is quiet time for the horses at 10 a.m. If they are at their home track, Lopez might take a break until he returns at 3 to feed and clean. But being on the road at places like Churchill Downs or Pimlico requires 24/7 dedication to the care and well being of his horses.
Lopez met Goldencents at Del Mar in 2012. He said he was a “dumpling” and is proud that he has matured enough “to run with the big boys.” He set about teaching him like he was a kid and taught him how to trust. A relationship between a groom and a horse is extremely intimate. The grooms are trained to take care of the horses like athletes. Mora explained the relationship further by saying, “The horse loves his care taker, but he knows his limitations because he is not a pet.  Because they are here to do performance as much as they can, which is something the horse also loves to do.”
It can be difficult because of the short duration a groom might have with a horse. They are the closest contact with a horse. But the horse will move on; it is inevitable. Mares leave to become broodmares.  Horses are claimed by other barns. Stallions are retired to the breeding shed. The relationship between horse and groom is extremely intense, and then it is over.
There is joy, though, when you have a talented horse like Goldencents. He travels well and acclimates quickly to a new environment. Lopez says that when they arrive at a new barn, the first thing Goldencents does is roll in his new stall.  While most horses stop, sniff and explore, Goldencents takes a good roll and relaxes immediately.
Lopez says he loves the horse as much as he loves his three children, Jayro, Cesar and Cristian. He came to the O’Neill barn in 2007, when Tommy Town Thoroughbreds transferred 28 horses to O’Neill for training.  Mora said: “I seen him trying hard.  We purchased Handsome Mike, and I told my foreman to give it to Lopez because he deserved to take care of a good horse. When the babies come every year, we put the babies with each groom, and we wish them good luck. So after that, Goldencents came up as his next one.”
Lopez came to the United States from Mexico looking for an opportunity. He said: “This is my passion.  This is my job, and I love what I do.”
Grooms often wear poker faces as they walk their horses from the barns to the paddock. All attention is on the horse, so it doesn’t spook or get too worked up before the race. At Churchill Downs, I was on the rail as Lopez walked by and yelled, “California is in the house.”  Lopez looked up and for one brief second, his face shined as bright as a sunny California day. There is something to be said about living your passion.  You can see it with Lopez as he is living the American Dream one horse at a time.
In a bucket-list moment, Julie June Stewart bought a ticket to the 2008 Belmont. She hasn’t stopped going to the races since. That is when she isn’t taking on a wildfire, hurricane, volcano or oil spill as the nation’s leading expert in disaster airspace coordination. She recently won third place in the 2012 Thoroughbred Times fiction contest with her suicide prevention story “Moses Finds A Jockey.”

Sure, it’s fun to traverse a city in 36 hours or explore some far-flung land over a luxurious two weeks. But when it comes to vacations, sometimes it’s nice to just pick a spot and stay put. If that’s what you’re in the mood for, the
Wheatleigh Hotel
, in Lenox, Mass. is the place for you. It’s not new, or of the moment, or even remotely cool, and that’s exactly the point.
Built in 1893 by a wealthy financier as a wedding gift to his daughter, the estate, modeled after a 16th-century Florentine palazzo, is nestled on 22 picturesque acres in the Berkshires. Architects Calvin Tsao and Zack McKown renovated the 19-room hotel in 2011, and clearly took future guests into thoughtful consideration. The suites are sprawling, with private terraces overlooking landscaped grounds originally designed by Frederick Law Olmsted; the tubs are clawfoot; and the beds are just soft and stately enough to make you never want to get up. (Of course, if you do, there’s plenty in the area to see:
Tanglewood
is a five-minute walk away, while
Jacob’s Pillow
and
MASS MoCA
are within a 45-minute drive.) But what really makes this hotel so attractive is all the special services on offer. Want an outdoor massage under the evergreens? A picnic made up for an outdoor concert? A five-course dinner on your balcony? Private yoga in your room? All can be arranged, and should.
On a recent weekend getaway to the Wheatleigh, my husband and I made all sorts of plans while making the three-hour drive up from New York. We followed through on none of them — didn’t even take a dip in the secluded circular-shaped pool in the woods. Saturday night, we finally decided to venture out for dinner to
Bell & Anchor
, a newish restaurant in Great Barrington by Mark Firth, a founder of the Brooklyn hipster foodie mecca
Diner
. But after a few glasses of rosé on the lawn, as the sun began to set, we heard a violin begin to play. A guest had surprised his wife with a private concert on their terrace for the evening. We took one look at each other, and decided to order room service, served al fresco on silver platters to the distant sounds of Mozart. We were in bed by 10.
11 Hawthorne Road, Lenox, Mass.; (413) 637-0610;
wheatleigh.com

Raul Labrador.
Every time Republicans suffer a rejection of the most right-wing items on their agenda, a significant number decide they haven’t been sufficiently crazy. That was the conclusion that many Republicans drew from the defeat of Mitt Romney in 2012. And now that Republicans in Congress have been forced to surrender in their fight with President Obama over the budget, health care and the nation’s credit, some are drawing the same conclusion.
In this view, as Dylan Scott pointed out on
Talking Points Memo today
, it was not the far-right that caused Speaker John Boehner problems, it was those pesky moderates (whoever they may be).  ”I’m more upset with my Republican conference, to be honest with you,” said Rep. Raul Labrador, Republican of Idaho. “It’s been Republicans here who apparently always want to fight, but they want to fight the next fight, that have given Speaker Boehner the inability to be successful in this fight. So if anybody should be kicked out, it’s probably those Republicans.”
He said they “are unwilling to keep the promises they made to the American people. Those are the people who should be looking behind their back.”
I don’t really have any idea what Mr. Labrador thinks those promises were. Presumably they did not include withholding paychecks from federal workers and threatening to create a worldwide recession.
But in the view of this crowd, having the same fight again in an election year (which could happen since the debt ceiling was raised only until Feb. 15) could actually be a good thing. That’s not so shocking, I guess, coming from the bomb-throwing Tea Party wing, but the political blindness goes farther than that.
Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, for example, said the fight over the debt ceiling was good for Democrats, but for a peculiar reason. “It has been the best two weeks for the Democratic Party in recent times because they were out of the spotlight and didn’t have to showcase their ideas,” Mr. Graham said.
What Mr. Graham perceived as hiding was actually an exercise in not interrupting your enemy while he’s making a mistake. It was a good period for Democrats because Republicans
were
in the spotlight
and
showcasing their ideas. Or their lack of ideas, in the words of Jeb Bush, the former Florida governor who always seems on the verge of making a presidential run that never quite seems to materialize.
“We have to have an agenda, we just can’t be against what’s in front of Washington, D.C.,” Bush
said on MSNBC’s “Morning Joe” today
. “Much of what goes on in Washington is completely irrelevant to the lives of everyday people. I mean it’s just amazing.”

Russ Rowland
Krista Buccellato and Jared Loftin in “Gary Goldfarb, Master Escapist.”
We are all mangosteens.
Like most important works of musical theater set in high schools, “Gary Goldfarb: Master Escapist” has a social message, and there it is. The mangosteen is an odd and rare fruit, high in antioxidants, difficult to find and reportedly so delicious you could die and go to vegetarian heaven after the first bite.
Plus, as Gary and his mother observe, the name is nice because it sounds kind of Jewish.
Much of “Gary Goldfarb,” which is part of this year’s New York Musical Theater Festival, is bliss and a half. Jared Loftin is cuddly-adorable and poignant as Gary, an insecure, overweight Long Island teenager who dreams of becoming a renowned magician but is having trouble even being allowed to enter the school’s talent show.
He is regularly bullied by Kenny (James David Larson) and Tyler (Dimitri Moise); quietly worshiped by Penelope (Krista Buccellato), who wears glasses, stutters and is in a wheelchair; and loudly disdained by Cheryl Samatsinghar-Stein (Shoba Narayanan), an Indian-Jewish beauty, the hottest girl in school.
Adults give Gary trouble, too. His mother, Gilda (MaryAnne Piccolo), taunts him about the need to diet. The cafeteria lady (Ms. Piccolo in a blond wig and blue-green lipstick) tempts him with empty carbs. Coach Rimsore (Todd Thurston) is no help, distracted as he is by his lust for Cheryl, who is approaching her 18th birthday.
Imagine “High School Musical” with cruelty, cynicism (maybe Penelope won’t be able to walk even in heaven) and knives (Kenny has a cutting habit). The songs — which include  “There’s No Future in Fat,” “Gary Loves My Tater Tots” and “Jewish Mothers”  — feature lyrics about gay people and Chick-fil-A, Israel and Iran, and Bernard Madoff. One number rhymes “preggers” with “keggers.”
The clever perpetrators are Omri Schein, who did the irreverent book and lyrics, and James Olmstead, who wrote the catchy, nicely varied music. “Gary Goldfarb,” directed with style by John Znidarsic, is tremendous fun and does have a happy ending — betraying its cool with gusto — but the show seems extremely New Yorkish. Could tourists ever embrace it?
Well, “Avenue Q,” which won the best-musical Tony with jokes about ethnic bias and sexually active puppets, is still running.
“Gary Goldfarb: Master Escapist” continues at the Pershing Square Signature Center, 480 West 42nd Street, Manhattan, Wednesday at 1 p.m. and Saturday at 5 p.m.; nymf.org, (212) 352-3101.

Hillel Nahmad, right, leaving court last month, is accused of being part of a huge gambling ring.
The all-night games were held in rarefied settings like a suite at the Plaza Hotel. One pink chip was worth $25,000. Masseuses were on hand to help relieve the tension, while the players were fueled by food and drink. And the stakes climbed into the stratosphere, with as much as $2 million on the table to be lost or won.

At one game, in an apartment in a glass condominium tower on Fifth Avenue, as cards fluttered and chips clattered across the table, its organizers suspected that a new player did not belong, though he had arrived with a regular. The two men were asked to leave. Turned out the organizers were right: The new player was an undercoverF.B.I.agent.
At roughly the same time, some of the people who helped organize the poker games were taking in breathtaking wagers on college and professional sports. One man bet $300,000 on last yearâs Super Bowl â and lost. Another placed a $1 million wager on another sporting event.
The description of the poker games and the wagers were among the details found in hundreds of conversations and text messages secretly captured by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, exposing the shadowy and illegal world of high-stakes gambling in New York City.
The recordings, according to court papers, were made over the last two years during an investigation into what federal prosecutors in Manhattan have characterized as two related multimillion-dollar money-laundering and gambling rings.
One of the gambling operations, which prosecutors say was led in part by the scion of a New York family that has wielded enormous power in the art market, with one of the largest collections of Impressionist and Modernist works in the world, was based in New York and Los Angeles, and served hedge fund titans, real estate magnates, celebrities and athletes.
The other, which prosecutors said was led by a Russian organized crime figure, catered to wealthy Russians living in Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere.
The scion of the New York family is Hillel Nahmad, 34, known as Helly, who was indicted in the case, along with 33 other people, on April 16; he is charged with racketeering, gambling and money laundering. He was released on bail.
The course of the investigation is detailed in hundreds of pages of wiretap and search-warrant affidavits.
Mr. Nahmadâs lawyers,Benjamin Brafmanand Paul Shechtman, say their client has done nothing wrong. Mr. Brafman declined to discuss his clientâs secretly recorded conversations, which included one in which he speaks of using the familyâs art business as a cover to move around illicit money.
In it, Mr. Nahmad advises a woman to wire $150,000 to the bank account of his father, David (who was not charged), suggesting she lie about the reason, saying, âYou just be like, Oh yeah, I bought a, you know, Picasso drawing or something.â
Mr. Brafman said, âItÂ  is a mistake to draw any negative inference orÂ  conclusion about a case or a particular defendant based on isolated taped conversations taken out of context.â Among page after page of mundane conversations about gambling and recordings of Mr. Nahmad taking bets over his cellphone were glimpses of a strange world of greed, gamblers and two classes of bettors: Those who kept wagering and who, it seemed, never ran out of money; and those who kept wagering, though it seemed they had none.
Because several of the men accused of operating the gambling rings are related â a father, Vadim Trincher, and his two sons, Illya and Eugene â some of the wiretapped conversations have an oddly homespun feel to them, even as others revealed the thuggery and threats of violence some ring members used to pressure those who would not pay.
âHave the guy call my dad tmrw at 10 a.m. he will connect him to the guy in Moscow,â Eugene Trincher tells another man in a text message. Another time, a defendant in the case sends Eugene a text about a money pickup in Las Vegas: âUr dad still need me to pick up cash in lv?â
Another man wrote to Illya to tell him that his father was cleaning up at a poker game at the Plaza in the early hours of one January morning, saying âYour dad is eating people up.â He added later: âPops won a big pot this past half, donât forget to remind him to tip the dealers, ha-ha!â

Sometimes it’s useful to know something about a critic’s frame of mind when he or she sits down to write a review. So let me confess that as I’m typing these sentences, the contents of an overnight delivery of delicacies fromRuss & Daughters,the Lower East Side purveyors of smoked fish and other appetizing items, are spread across my writing desk.
Mark Russ Federman, and his wife, Maria, owners of Russ & Daughters, in 2000.
Reflections and Recipes From the House That Herring Built
Illustrated. 205 pages. Schocken Books. $25.95.
Russ & Daughters, on East Houston Street, the Lower East Side, purveyors of smoked fish and other traditional foods.
I didn’t go wild. I ordered three schmaltz herring, a container of whitefish salad, 10 bialys. But I’ve surrounded these soloists with an orchestra: tomato and onion slices, a hunk of cream cheese, capers, a wedge of lemon. Within a few hours I’ll contemplate the tapering line between nosh and nap.
I’m compelled to admit all this because I’m in a frame of mind to forgive almost anything about the new book that made me hungry enough to place this order, “Russ & Daughters: Reflections and Recipes From the House That Herring Built.” When you can muster provisions like these, who cares if you can write?
Happily, there’s little to forgive. “Russ & Daughters” is a good story well told, packed with zinging Yiddishisms and better-than-average jokes that bubble up organically. You soak in it, like a brine, until you’re pleasantly pickled.
This book’s author is Mark Russ Federman, a grandson of the store’s founder, Joel Russ. Mr. Federman ran Russ & Daughters for more than three decades before turning it over in 2009 to the fourth generation: his daughter, Niki, and a nephew, Josh.
Mark Federman’s voice pops from the page. He gets the basic story told, about how his impoverished grandfather Joel arrived in the United States from Poland and began peddling herring from a pushcart before opening a small storefront in 1914. Joel’s three pretty daughters — Hattie, Ida and Anne — eventually came to work in the shop, which became known as Russ & Daughters in 1935.
Mr. Federman is Anne Russ’s son. He relates theups and downsof running a business on the gritty Lower East Side of Manhattan over the course of a century. He’s good on what it feels like to have food culture grow in status, to see his blue-collar family venerated. Most of the other 20 or 30 smoked fish shops that once populated the neighborhood didn’t make it past the second generation, for a simple reason: “No one wanted their kids in the business.”
Mr. Federman himself attended Georgetown Law School and planned to flee the family profession. When he was called back to the store to help out a bit, this happened: “The first day I took up my place behind the counter was the last day I practiced law.”
He was adept at the two things that matter most at Russ & Daughters: slicing and schmoozing. The perfect schmooze, he declares, “must be a seamless resumption of your last conversation, even if the customer’s last visit was six months ago.” A truly great schmoozer, he adds, “will attempt to bring other customers into the schmooze. When two or more customers are introduced into the schmooze, they are likely to discover things they have in common.”
Beware faking it, though. “You’re either born a schmoozer or you’re not,” Mr. Federman says. For the rest of us he offers this solace: “The schmoozing gene will soon be mapped.”
The best parts of “Russ & Daughters” arrive when Mr. Federman is simply and nonlinearly telling stories. Here he is on his sometimes brusque father: “He taught me how to ride a bike by letting go of it at the top of a steep hill.”
He notes that his grandfather wasn’t the romantic type. About his grandmother Bella he reports: “Joel called his wife Zug, which loosely translates from the Yiddish as ‘Hey, you.’ ”
He notes that Joel’s daughters didn’t have much of a social life. For one thing, they were too tired after long days in the shop. For another, they “recognized that they smelled a bit too fishy.”
Joel didn’t arrange his daughter’s marriages, Mr. Federman writes, but he “did retain what is called in business today the right of first refusal.”
Here’s how Joel evaluated a potential son-in-law: “Was he strong enough to schlep barrels of herring? Smart enough to add up a column of numbers on a brown paper bag? Could he make change? Would he look good behind the counter?” If so, “Fine, you can marry him.”
While Mr. Federman’s own daughter is now in the family business, his son, Noah, is practicing medicine. About this he says: “As far as I know, I am the only Jewish father who was disappointed that his kid became a doctor. I was thinking sturgeon, not surgeon.”
Not that he is opposed to higher education. Niki attended the Institut d’Études Politiques in Paris. During school breaks she came back to work the counter.
There have been changes at Russ & Daughters. Slivers of hipness have sneaked in. One day not long ago, after he’d been away on vacation, Mr. Federman reports, “I overheard a customer step up to the counter and ask for a ‘Super Heeb.’ ”
He asked, “What the hell is that about?” His nephew pointed to the sandwich menu, which now said in bold capital letters: “NEW ITEM: THE SUPER HEEB. Sesame bagel, horseradish cream cheese, whitefish salad, and wasabi-flavored flying fish roe.”
Mr. Federman feared that members of his old clientele would be scandalized. They weren’t. The Super Heeb was a hit. These days you can order sandwicheswith names likethe Shtetl, the Meshugge and the Boychick.
Many people outside New York City first learned about Russ & Daughters fromCalvin Trillin,who began writing about the restaurant in his New Yorker food pieces in the 1970s and has supplied a lovely introduction to this book.
He regularly took his daughters there on Sunday mornings. Now he takes his granddaughters. He waits for the manager, Herman Vargas, to produce slices of smoked salmon “thin enough to read The New York Times through.” Mr. Trillin adds: “Not the big-print edition; I’m talking about the regular.”

Disunion
follows the Civil War as it unfolded.
Tags:
David Farragut
,
Galveston
,
The Civil War
,
the hatteras
Hon. Gideon Welles, Secretary of the Navy, Washington, D.C.
October 15, 1862
Sir: I am happy to inform you that Galveston, Corpus Christi, and Sabine City and the adjacent waters are now in our possession… I sent Commander W.B. Renshaw…to take Galveston, which he did in the shortest time, and without the loss of a man.
– D.G. Farragut, Rear-Admiral, Commanding, Western Gulf Blockading Squadron
As the year 1862 ended, Union naval forces had consolidated effective control of much of the Texas Gulf Coast. From Sabine Pass in the North to the mouth of the Rio Grande, almost all of the roughly 450 miles of Texas coastline were safely in their hands.  During that year, minor engagements at Corpus Christi, Galveston and Sabine Pass had effectively secured the coastline from most Confederate shipping.
The capture of Galveston was the key. Texas was a large cotton producer, and its ability to trade with Mexico, Cuba and other nations through its Gulf ports — mainly Galveston — was crucial to finance the Confederate war effort. So when Union forces under Commander William Renshaw captured Galveston without loss on Oct. 9, Farragut was understandably enthusiastic.
But naval fortunes can change as quickly as the wind. As the new year dawned, the Union navy was rocked by two disasters. Beginning with the loss of the celebrated ironclad U.S.S. Monitor in a gale off Cape Hatteras on New Year’s Eve, followed by the successful surprise
Confederate recapture of the Port of Galveston
on New Year’s morning, Union naval forces in one day suffered two devastating psychological and military setbacks.
The tragic loss of the Monitor was more of an emotional blow to the country than a real military setback.  The Monitor gained enduring fame by her standoff duel with the Confederate ironclad C.S.S. Virginia (formerly the U.S.S. Merrimac) in Hampton Roads, Va., after the Virginia had easily destroyed two Union warships the day before. The Monitor was rightly hailed as the savior of the Union fleet, and she came to symbolize Union ingenuity and technological superiority.  On her heels, a whole fleet of “Monitors” came off northern shipyard docks to bolster the Union war effort.
The loss of the port of Galveston, on the other hand, if not rectified, would be a strategic disaster. Farragut longed to be there himself to lead the Union vessels, but instead appointed his close associate Commodore Henry H. Bell to shore up and command the Galveston fleet, and accomplish the recapture of Galveston. Farragut sent what reinforcements he could spare from the Mississippi River force to enhance the Galveston fleet.  Joining that effort was the U.S.S. Hatteras.
The Hatteras was a twin sidewheel merchant steamer, converted to military use in 1861.  Her captain, Lt. Cmdr. Homer C. Blake, was a graduate of the first midshipman’s class at the United States Naval Academy in 1846.  During 1862, Blake and the Hatteras saw successful action as a blockade vessel along the Florida and Louisiana coasts, capturing more than a dozen Confederate blockade runners, and establishing the Hatteras as a steady influence against more lightly armed vessels. On the late afternoon of Jan. 10, 1863, Blake and the Hatteras joined the sparse blockade squadron marking time just off Galveston Harbor.
U.S. Naval Historical Center
The Alabama engages the Hatteras off Galveston, Tex., on Jan. 11, 1863.
Another ship was lurking off Galveston that day, though. Carrying more sail, more steam and more firepower than any of the Union vessels, the notorious Confederate raider C.S.S. Alabama, under the command of the aggressive and vainglorious Capt. Raphael Semmes, had crossed the Gulf of Mexico from Yucatan to disrupt an expected expeditionary force of Union General Nathaniel Banks. Semmes in his memoirs noted that:
My object, in running into the Gulf of Mexico, was to strike a blow at Banks’ expedition, which was then fitting out for the invasion of Texas. This gentleman, who had been a prominent Massachusetts politician, but who had no sort of military talent, had risen to the surface with other scum, amid the bubbling and boiling of the Yankee cauldron, and was appointed by “Honest Abe” to subjugate Texas.
Notwithstanding her captain’s oceanic ego, the Alabama presented a real threat to Union shipping.  Like the German U-Boats that followed some 80 years later, the Confederate raiders C.S.S. Alabama and C.S.S. Florida, built secretly in England and heavily armed, terrorized United States shipping in the Civil War. Between them, the Alabama and the Florida sank or captured more than 100 commercial vessels in a 26-month period in 1862-64.  As a carefully planned Confederate strategy, however, none of those vessels were armed U.S. ships of war.  The Florida’s captain, John Maffitt, while
under repairs in Mobile Bay
, explained the strategy in his ship’s log on Dec 1, 1862:
‘Tis to the interest of the Confederacy that we get out intact, as my orders are to assail their commerce only…As the Alabama and Florida are the only two cruisers we have just now, it would be a perfect absurdity to tilt against their more than three hundred, for the Federals would gladly sacrifice fifty armed ships to extinguish the two Confederates.
Thus, both the Alabama and the Florida — each scarcely four months in service — had been  careful to avoid direct conflict with armed U.S. naval vessels.
Until now.
On the afternoon of Jan. 11,  five Union warships drifted in an uncertain flotilla just off Galveston Light. With no sufficient forces to retake the port, the blockade squadron seemed content with a show of military force sufficient to make its presence known, occasionally exploding a shell above the city.  The squadron’s unexpected presence foiled the Alabama’s plans to destroy an unarmed merchant fleet intended to supply Banks. But Captain Semmes quickly devised an alternative strategy:
I certainly had not come all the way into the Gulf of Mexico, to fight five ships of war…. Whilst I was pondering the difficulty, the enemy himself, happily, came to my relief; for pretty soon the look-out again called from aloft, and said, ‘One of the steamers, sir, is coming out in chase of us.’ The Alabama had given chase pretty often, but this was the first time she had been chased. It was just the thing I wanted, however, for I at once conceived the design of drawing this single ship of the enemy far enough away from the remainder of her fleet, to enable me to decide a battle with her before her consorts could come to her relief.
Upon spying the Alabama, Bell on his flagship U.S.S. Brooklyn signaled Blake on the Hatteras to investigate “the strange sail”; and the Hatteras immediately gave chase.  Aware after a couple of hours that his slow-moving ship was gaining on the sleek Alabama, Blake guessed the Alabama’s strategy. He nonetheless continued to pursue the raider without cover from any other vessels in the blockading squadron, perhaps underestimating the Alabama’s massive firepower.  After a “chase” of several hours, the Alabama suddenly heaved to and furled her sails some 20 miles south of Galveston, out of sight — but not out of earshot — of the Union forces.
Anticipating her rival’s actions, the Hatteras approached cautiously, with every gun manned. Blake hailed the Alabama, demanding to know what vessel she was. “This is her Britannic Majesty’s steamer Petrel,” the raider falsely replied.  As soon as the Hatteras lowered a boat to go aboard the Alabama and confirm her identity, the Alabama from 100  yards away announced her true identity and simultaneously let loose a crippling broadside from her 100-pound gun, her 68-pounder, with a couple of 32-pounders to boot. Both the Alabama and the Hatteras recoiled under the shock of the surprise broadside, but the Hatteras immediately fired back. The two ships steamed side by side, jockeying for position, exchanging broadsides for about 15 minutes, sometimes only 50 yards apart.  Under now-darkened skies, the sounds and lights of the furious engagement were heard and seen by the blockade squadron in Galveston, and a Union vessel as far as 80 miles away in Sabine Pass noted the flashes in the sky in the ship’s log.
As would be expected, the Alabama’s powerful guns quickly won the day. As the Hatteras became disabled, caught fire and took on water, Blake fired a gun of surrender and the Alabama sent boats for her crew just before the ship sank in 60 feet of water.  Two Hatteras crewman, the Irish-born fireman John G. Cleary and the coal heaver William Healy, died in the battle and were entombed with the ship. Blake was the last man to leave the sinking Hatteras, stepping onto a longboat even as her decks were awash.
Immediately upon hearing the distant gunfire, the Brooklyn and two other gunboats from the blockade squadron steamed to the Hatteras’s aid, but were unable to locate the combatants at night. Circling back towards Galveston the next day, the Brooklyn found the remains of the Hatteras upright in 9½ fathoms of water, her topmasts protruding  and “a United States naval pennant flying gaily” in the breeze.  Even in defeat, the Hatteras had not struck her colors.
Meanwhile, the triumphant Alabama took the Hatteras’s 118 officers and crew prisoners and set sail for Jamaica, depositing the survivors nine days later in Port Royal. Finding their way under the protection of the United States Consul in Jamaica, Blake and his remaining crew were soon returned to the United States. Although the Alabama was the clear victor, it cost more than $85,000 to repair the damage done by the Hatteras.
The short but pitched battle between the Hatteras and the Alabama was unique, and had long-lasting military consequences. The Hatteras was the first — indeed the only — Union warship sunk by combat in the Gulf of Mexico.  It became the only military vessel among the 100 victims of the Alabama and the Florida, demonstrating the inherent limitations of converting merchant ships to military use. And as a result of the engagement, now having lost his third Galveston warship in less than two weeks, Farragut was forced to pull back his forces.
This final disaster at Galveston depressed Farragut. In a Jan. 13 letter to a friend, while anchored in his flagship Hartford off New Orleans, he confided:
“Yesterday was a sad day for me. I went to see [General] Banks, and he handed me a dispatch from the bar, announcing the loss of the Hatteras. … Well I hope we shall soon have some good luck, for I am sick of disasters. I was in hopes Bell would retake Galveston,  but the loss of the Hatteras throws him back.”
Farragut’s son Loyall attended him in the evenings, as a guest of the admiral,  and he closed the melancholy letter on behalf of his father:
“Father’s eyes have given out, so I will finish this letter. He has been very much worried at these things, but tries to bear it like a philosopher. He knows he has done all in his power to avert it, with the vessels at his disposal.”
The news did not improve, and on Feb. 13, in still another letter, Farragut complained: “Our disaster at Galveston has thrown us back, and done more injury to the Navy than all events of the war.” Farragut’s pessimism proved correct. While he personally would see great glory in later engagements, the loss of the Hatteras was the final straw on the Texas coast, as Galveston remained in Confederate hands for the balance of the war, eventually becoming the last remaining port under Confederate control.

Benny Andrews was born into a sharecropping family in Plainview, Ga., in 1930; went to a local college on a scholarship, dropped out, joined the Air Force and ended up at the Art Institute of Chicago, where, as one of the few black students, he felt ill at ease. By the end of the 1950s he was in New York, making figurative paintings that were also collages and sculptural reliefs built up from scraps of recycled clothing. The work, social and political in content, had little to do with mainstream styles of the day.
The 36 pictures atMichael Rosenfeldspan Andrews’s career. One of the earliest pieces, “Dinner Time” from 1965, is a straightforward oil-on-canvas domestic scene; “Liberty #6 (Study for Trash) (Bicentennial Series),” made six years later, is a symbolic depiction of a parade float carrying headless nude soldiers and a woozy blond, flag-swathed Lady Liberty. In the time between those pictures, Andrews (whodiedin 2006) was active in the civil rights movement, taught art in a New York jail, and helped found the Black Emergency Cultural Coalition, which campaigned to have major museums recognize African-American art.
Allegory and genre, sometimes combined, remained his dominant modes; experiments with high-relief fabric collage continued. In subject Andrews’s art continued to be of its time; in form it never was, which limited its circulation. Rosenfeld, working with Andrews’s widow, the artist Nene Humphrey, is working to give the career the visibility it deserves. An institutional survey, accompanied by an edition of Andrews’s invaluable and voluminous journals, is in order, letting us see an important body of work and an important American life in full.
Pop Art’s continuation and subversion of the still life tradition is not exactly a new idea, given that the first museum show devoted to Pop — at the Pasadena Art Museum in California in 1962 — was titled “New Painting of Common Objects.” This show, organized by the art historian John Wilmerding, is accompanied by an ostentatious catalog at least partly designed to encourage sales, and is installed almost as gracelessly as an auction-house display. Still, it has clarity on its side, thanks to Mr. Wilmerding’s thematicdivisions: flowers and plants, household objects, body parts and clothes, and food and drink. It also expands beyond the usual Pop suspects to include the slyly three-dimensional paintings (depicting roses and lima beans) of Marjorie Strider and a soft sewn-and-stuffed-fabric coffee-table still life by Jann Haworth, as well as works by John Wesley, Stephen Antonakos, Robert Arneson and H. C. Westermann. The vacuum-cleaner piece by Jeff Koons is perhaps an expansion too far.
But mainly this is a great cherry-picking exhibition, most notable for a handful of unfamiliar, rarely exhibited or outstanding works. Among these are Jim Dine’s“Five Feet of Colorful Tools”(1962), with its playful confusion of objects, shadows and silhouettes; Vija Celmins’s giant hyper-real sculptures of a pencil and a rubber eraser, as spellbinding as ever; and Marisol Escobar’s carved wood (with drawing and painting) portrait of Andy Warhol. Edward Kienholz’s “Cement TV,” a portable television neatly coated with cement, seems sardonically anti-Pop. The show’s oddest surprise may be “Steel Plant II Rubber,” a welded-steel representation of a rubber (not a steel) plant by Larry Rivers, from 1959. The single most thrilling sight by far is Roy Lichtenstein’s “Black Flowers” from 1961, a somewhat crudely rendered masterpiece that merges painting, drawing and commercial printing. At once exuberant and desiccated, and on loan from the Los Angeles collector Eli Broad, it justifies the whole show. ROBERTA SMITH

A quiet revolution underway for some time now at Columbia University’sMiller Theatercontinued apace on Thursday night, when the enterprising new-music ensembleEither/Ordevoted a Composer Portraits program to works byAnna Thorvaldsdottir. Under the watch ofMelissa Smey, the theater’s executive director since 2009, Miller has devoted considerable resources to presenting music by female composers, both established and emerging — and has done so with a lack of fanfare that characterizes the initiative as no anomaly, but simply business as usual.

Ms. Smey, welcoming the audience from the stage, said that Ms. Thorvaldsdottir had been on her wish list for several years. That statement underscored Ms. Smey’s agile reflexes: Ms. Thorvaldsdottir, now 36, is just starting to establish an international profile. Born and initially schooled in Iceland, she completed her training at the University of California, San Diego, in 2011.“Rhizoma,”her ear-opening debut CD, came out that same year.
Anyone wondering how Jack Miller’s Tractor of Schoharie, N.Y., earned a citation in the program was quickly enlightened during “into — second self,” which opened the concert. With hisses, murmurs and thumps resounding from French-horn players, trombonists and percussionists positioned throughout the theater, one performer, Matthew Gold, rolled a large metal wheel around the stage: slowly, deliberately and for aural effect.
When I heard the Iceland Symphony Orchestra givethis work’s premierein a much larger hall in Reykjavik last April, its gestures sounded distant and detached. Miller’s relative intimacy and dry acoustics provided the uncanny sensation of being enveloped in the music’s minute doings, and jostled by its outbursts.
Two pieces demonstrated Ms. Thorvaldsdottir’s fluid approach to the piano. In “[one],” Richard Carrick played resonant notes on the keyboard, but as often busied himself with the piano’s subtly amplified innards. The percussionist David Shively, with his back to the audience, leaned into the instrument throughout, eliciting eerie moans, sighs and rumbles.
The piano also served percussive ends in “Ro/Serenity,” with a string quartet, bass flute and bass clarinet fusing into a gaseous body. Melodic flickers and packets of simple harmony escaped the ensemble’s gravitational pull repeatedly, only to be sucked back in.
After a brief onstage interview with Ms. Thorvaldsdottir, conducted by Mr. Carrick, “Tactility,” for harp and percussion, gave further evidence of a seemingly boundless textural imagination. Amplification made tiny patters, wisps and thumps sing out, while also facilitating further sounds unattainable from purely acoustic implements.
As Mr. Shively and the ingenious harpist Zeena Parkins worked at the back of the darkened platform, their sounds emanated with vivid presence from loudspeakers on either side of the stage. It may have made sense for logistical reasons, but had an effect of unintended distance, with the players turned specters in a shadow puppet ritual.
“Hrim,” which ended the program, has become Ms. Thorvaldsdottir’s signature piece, with three prior performances in the United States (includingone in New York). Understandably so: In just eight minutes, this chamber orchestra work perfectly encapsulates her uncanny knack for conjuring the natural world — not through quaint, picturesque mimicry, but with potent evocations of elemental power, flux and potential.
The next event in the Composer Portraits series, focusing on Roger Reynolds, is on Feb. 22 at the Miller Theater, Broadway at 116th Street, Morningside Heights; 212-854-7799, millertheatre.com.

When a pro-am pair wins a tournament, usually the professional offers a deal featuring himself. So it is always refreshing to see something played or defended well by the amateur.
The diagramed deal was sent to me by three-time national champion Rick Zucker of Dobbs Ferry, N.Y. He and his partner, Sheila Cornstein of New York City, won the Wednesday Senior Pairs at the District 3 Winter Regional in Rye Brook, N.Y., in January. They finished one-third of a board ahead of William Hoffman of Irvington, N.Y., and Paul Lewis of White Plains, N.Y. Third were Judith Hess of Fairfield, Conn., and Nicholas France of Spring Valley, N.Y.
The diagramed deal occurred during the first round of the two-session event.
In the auction, two hearts was a reverse. (Opener bid one suit, responder did not raise that suit, then opener rebid in a new suit. If responder wished to give simple preference to opener’s first suit, he would have been forced to bid at the three-level — here, three diamonds. After a one-level response, opener’s reverse promises 18 to 20 high-card points, or a very good 17.) Three hearts was game-forcing, showing four-card support. Then, after a couple of control-bids (cue-bids) at the four-level, North-South stopped just in time at four hearts.
West led a club. Cornstein (South) won in her hand, cashed the spade ace and diamond ace, crossruffed two diamonds and two spades, took her second club trick, then ruffed another diamond in the dummy. That was the first nine tricks in and Cornstein still had the king-queen of hearts in her hand for a tenth trick.
Plus 620 was worth 12.21 matchpoints out of 17.
There were other ways to get home, eventually endplaying West with a trump to lead a diamond into South’s ace-queen, but Cornstein’s line was effective.
When play concluded, West, five-time world champion Gail Greenberg, congratulated Cornstein on her line of play, which brought a big smile to South’s face and got the tournament off to the perfect start for the eventual winners.
Often, when in a 4-4 fit, if trumps are breaking badly, you do best not to touch them. But, of course, only by playing on trumps will you find out that they are splitting unfavorably. It is a classic Catch-22.

“L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato” returns to Lincoln Center.
Mark Morris created “L’Allegro,il Penseroso ed il Moderato” during the three years his company was resident at the Théâtre Royal de la Monnaie in Brussels. It was 1988, he was 32 and, for the first time, had an 1,100-seat opera house, an orchestra and a costume department at his disposal. He used it all with relish. “L’Allegro,” which returns to Lincoln Center this week, wasn’t immediately acclaimed by the local critics. (Mr. Morris’s biographer, Joan Acocella, quotes one review: “Where is the profundity?”) But it has become Mr. Morris’s most famous piece, celebrated for its innocence, exuberance and how it suggests the physical embodiment of ideal worlds. The work is set to the 1740 Handel oratorio from which it takes its title, and which uses the texts of Milton’s “L’Allegro” and “Il Penseroso,” portraits of the joyful and contemplative minds. Filled with nymphs and shepherds, gods and humans, hunters and lovers, the dance is beautiful, lavish and funny. It is, as Ms. Acocella writes, “a hymn to the unity of poetry, music and dance.” (7:30 p.m. Thursday to Saturday, David H. Koch Theater, 212-496-0600,davidhkochtheater.com.)

On the plane back to Washington, in her pink Chanel suit, caked with her husbandâs blood, Jackie Kennedy resisted all suggestions from aides that she clean herself up. Instead, she just said, âLet them see what theyâve done.â

Wearing the bloodstained pink suit that has become one of the artifacts of Nov. 22, 1963, Ms. Kennedy arrived at Andrews Air Force Base and was escorted by her brother-in-law Robert F. Kennedy.
But for the half century since John F. Kennedyâs assassination in Dallas on Nov. 22, 1963, the most famous artifact from that day, one of the most recognizable articles of clothing ever worn, has been seen by almost no one. Now preserved by the National Archives in a climate-controlled vault outside of Washington, it is subject to Kennedy family restrictions that it not be seen for almost a century more.
If there is a single item that captures both the shame and the violence that erupted that day, and the glamour and artifice that preceded it, it is Jackie Kennedyâs bloodstained pink suit, a tantalizing window on fame and fashion, her allure and her steely resolve, the things we know about her and the things we never quite will.
That Mrs. Kennedy is so closely linked to an item of clothing is fitting. In nearly three years as first lady, she had gained universal celebrity for her youthful style. Politically, it meant huge crowds whenever she accompanied the president. But for Mrs. Kennedy, who felt vulnerable, fashion gave her a sense of separation from the publicâs gaze. It was armor.
So even on that day, before the horror of what ensued, to look at Mrs. Kennedy was to be drawn inevitably to the pink suit, a line-for-line copy of a classic cardigan-style Chanel with navy lapels. The suit came from Chez Ninon, a Park Avenue salon that created many of her clothes, following her taste for simple lines. She wore it at least six other times, including on a 1962 visit to London and that same year to greet the prime minister of Algeria.
Fifty years ago, at noon in Dallas, Clint Hill, who was the Secret Service agent assigned to Mrs. Kennedy, thought the pink suit looked fluorescent against the dark blue of the car carrying the president and the first lady.
âShe stood out so much in the car because of the color of that suit,â said Mr. Hill, who has released a new account of the killing, âFive Days in November,â in time for the anniversary. âIt was like the sun just illuminated it.â
Now preserved in its vault, the pink suit and its accessories, still stained, the stockings blood-powdered and folded in a white towel, remain essentially unchanged from the day of the assassination. Only the outfitâs matching pillbox hat and white kid gloves are missing, lost in the chaos of that day.
Although the National Archives has kept the suit and accessories, including navy shoes, bag and navy blouse, since 1964, when they arrived in a dress box, the items legally belonged after her death to Caroline Kennedy as her motherâs surviving heir. So a deed of gift was made in 2003 with the provision that the suit would not be seen by the public until 2103. Through her office, Ms. Kennedy declined to comment.
Over the years, the Kennedy family has sought to avoid the sensational treatment of assassination artifacts, and that is the explicit intent of the 100-year restriction. Nonetheless, Martha Murphy, chief of special access at the archives, said Mrs. Kennedyâs clothes are the only items in the assassination collection with this specific restriction.
By comparison, scholars and researchers who meet special criteria of the archives may view President Kennedyâs clothing and the rifle used by Lee Harvey Oswald. To the best of anyoneâs knowledge, access to Mrs. Kennedyâs suit for research purposes has never been granted.
After Mrs. Kennedy returned to the White House, early on Nov. 23, her clothing was put in a bag, presumably by her personal maid, Providencia Paredes, and soon after placed in a dress box. Records show that it arrived at the archives sometime before July 1964, accompanied by an unsigned note on the stationery of Mrs. Kennedyâs mother, Janet Auchincloss.

Harold Grall checks his cornfield in Dumas, part of a project to show farmers how to use less water for irrigation.
DUMAS, Tex. â Deep in the Texas Panhandle, where the decline of theOgallala Aquiferhas left farmers fearful for their future, Harold Grall is hoping his field of tiny green corn plants will survive with minimal watering.
